title: Slavery in the ancient world
summary: The University of Chicago's study of slaves and households in the Near East examines slavery across almost four millennia, beginning in early Mesopotamia. The Code of Ur-Nammu, about 2100 to 2050 BCE, is the oldest surviving law code, and the slightly later Code of Lipit-Ishtar deals with debt enslavement among other disputes.

uncertainty.note: Early cuneiform records from the early third millennium BCE onward document chattel slavery and captive labor, culminating in statutory codification in the Code of Ur-Nammu c. 2100–2050 BCE.

as_recorded.value: The volume contains micro-historical examinations of slavery in contexts spanning almost four millennia.
The Code of Ur-Nammu (circa 2100-2050 BCE) is the oldest extant law code in the world.

when.display: documented from c. 2100 BCE; practised for millennia

where.modern_name: Near East; stand-in pin at Ur, Iraq
where.historical_name: Ur and the city-states of Sumer, southern Mesopotamia; institutional slavery also emerged in contemporary Early Dynastic Egypt

importance.justification: The institutionalization of chattel bondage and coerced human labor created an enduring system of social subjugation across early agrarian states and empires.

audience_note: Covers chattel bondage, captive enslavement, forced institutional labor, and corporal subjugation in early ancient states.

related.because: State formation created the legal and military apparatus that captured, codified, and enforced human bondage.
